nature-eco-680.title: Marine heatwaves: when the sea runs hot for weeks
nature-eco-680.text:
In 2011 a surge of warm water off Western Australia killed back kelp forests, and the event gave scientists a name for what they had seen. A marine heatwave is a period of abnormally high sea surface temperatures for a given season and place. A 2016 study defined one as five or more days above the 90th percentile of a 30-year baseline.

Unlike land heatwaves, these events can cover vast areas, last weeks to years and reach below the surface. They are rated Category 1 (moderate) to 4 (extreme) and named by place and year, such as Mediterranean 2003. Drivers include local processes, El Niño, which contributed to The Blob in the Northeast Pacific, decadal oscillations and {{ref:nature-hist-007}}.

The IPCC's 2019 report said marine heatwaves had doubled in frequency and grown longer, more intense and more extensive. They are projected to be four times as frequent in 2081-2100 as in 1995-2014 under low emissions, and eight times under high emissions. They destroy seagrass, coral and kelp habitat, shift species ranges, and cost an estimated USD 6.6 billion in fisheries losses from 1985 to 2022. Many reefs face irreversible phase shifts above 1.5 °C of warming, the end point of {{ref:nature-eco-459}}.

nature-eco-712.title: Free trade versus infant industries: an unsettled dispute
nature-eco-712.text: Should poor countries open their markets, or shield their young industries? Economists disagree. Paul Bairoch argues that liberalism forced on the Global South in the 19th century delayed its industrialization. Joseph Stiglitz notes that the US and Japan built their wealth by protecting infant industries, while the IMF and World Bank demand open markets from vulnerable economies. Ha-Joon Chang adds that tariffs were only one tool of now-developed countries, alongside export subsidies, monopoly rights, cartel arrangements and directed credits. The question matters for how {{ref:nature-eco-711}} is judged.

nature-eco-738.title: Self-reinforcing loops in markets and societies
nature-eco-738.text: A Ponzi scheme grows by feeding on its own growth, and that is why it ends in collapse. Positive feedback in socioeconomic systems means loops in which an outcome strengthens its own cause, as in markets, populations and institutions. Real loops are usually limited by some constraint; left unchecked, a positive loop destroys its system, and a negative loop usually steps in sooner or later. Systemic risk is the danger that an amplifying, leveraged loop poses to a whole system. Agriculture and human population can be seen as a pair of reinforcing loops that may end in catastrophe as easily available phosphate runs out. Drought works the same way: less rain dries soils, plants transpire less, and evapotranspiration falls.

nature-eco-710.title: The detritus cycle: eating the same meal twice
nature-eco-710.text: In the detritus cycle, the same material is eaten again and again. It is a food chain linking detritivores, detritus and the microorganisms that multiply on it. Detritivores digest the protein-rich microorganisms on the detritus and excrete mostly complex carbohydrates. Microbes recolonise that dung before it is eaten again. Each pass thins and fractures the material, making it easier for microorganisms to use. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi then recycle what is left. The cycle also plays a large part in purifying organic material carried in by rivers.

nature-eco-705.title: Biological deserts: empty of life, not of water
nature-eco-705.text: Some of the emptiest places on Earth are drenched. A biological desert is defined by a lack of life rather than a lack of water. Examples include ocean deserts at the centers of gyres, and hypoxic or anoxic waters such as dead zones.

nature-eco-708.title: How desert dust storms begin
nature-eco-708.text: Dust storms begin where the ground has nothing to hold it down. Sand and dust storms are natural events in arid regions where the land lacks a covering of vegetation. They usually start in desert margins, where the finer material has already been blown away elsewhere. Steady wind makes fine particles vibrate, and at greater speeds some are lifted into the air stream.

nature-eco-706.title: Farming the desert with water and manure
nature-eco-706.text: North Africa has farmed deserts for a long time, and water is the limit. Where water stress holds growth back, irrigation is the key. Techniques include drip irrigation, and organic residues or animal manures as fertilizer. Once fertility is built up, continued cropping protects the soil from wind and other erosion.

nature-eco-707.title: Deserts as solar power sites
nature-eco-707.text: Part of the appeal of deserts is what they lack: cloud. Deserts are increasingly seen as sources of solar energy, partly because of their low cloud cover. Many solar plants have been built in the Mojave Desert, including the Solar Energy Generating Systems and the Ivanpah Solar Power Facility.

nature-eco-704.title: Polar deserts: dry because they are cold
nature-eco-704.text: Antarctica is the world's largest cold desert, about 98% ice sheet and 2% barren rock. Polar deserts are dry because of low precipitation and marginal evaporation, not a lack of water. The McMurdo dry valleys lack rain, ice and snow and have desert features such as hypersaline lakes. There, extreme winds, not heat, desiccate the land.

nature-eco-698.title: Methane hydrates: a feared warming trigger that proved slow
nature-eco-698.text: Around 2008 there was serious concern that shallow Arctic hydrates could break down quickly. Methane hydrates are frozen compounds in which a large amount of methane is trapped in a water crystal structure, usually beneath ocean-floor sediments. The fear was a release that could cause 6 °C of warming within 80 years, a {{ref:nature-eco-014}} of the worst kind. Current research shows a calmer picture. Hydrates react very slowly to warming, and methane struggles to reach the atmosphere after seafloor dissociation.

nature-eco-697.title: The Planck response: Earth's built-in thermostat
nature-eco-697.text: A warmer Earth sheds heat faster, and that single fact steadies the whole climate. The Planck response is the extra thermal radiation objects emit as they warm, the most fundamental stabilizing feedback in the climate system. Infrared emission rises with the fourth power of absolute temperature, so a warmer Earth sends more radiation to space. It is sometimes called the no-feedback response, and it is included when calculating climate sensitivity even if treated apart from the radiative feedbacks.

nature-eco-690.title: Biomagnification: poisons that climb the food chain
nature-eco-690.text: A trace of mercury in a lake can become a danger on the dinner plate. Biomagnification is the rise in the concentration of a chemical or metal as it moves from one trophic level to the next. Methylmercury enters freshwater through industrial emissions and rain, and its concentration climbs the food web to levels dangerous to fish and to the humans who eat them. In some eutrophic systems the reverse happens. This is biodilution: contaminant concentration falls with trophic level because abundant algae and bacteria dilute it.

nature-eco-691.title: Hyperaccumulator plants that soak up metals
nature-eco-691.text: Some plants take up certain elements at up to 1000 times the level of their neighbors. Hyperaccumulators concentrate elements or their ions far above adjacent non-hyperaccumulators. That makes them candidates for removing heavy metals from contaminated sites such as abandoned mines, and phytomining of valuable metals has been considered. There is a downside: plants that concentrate low levels of selenium can threaten grazing animals.

nature-eco-702.title: Muirburn: burning moors for grouse
nature-eco-702.text: Muirburn is the burning of large areas of grouse moor in northern Great Britain. The fire kills trees and grasses, preventing natural succession. It leaves a mosaic of heather of different ages that supports very large red grouse populations for shooting. The cost is on the ground below. The peatlands are among the UK's largest carbon sinks, and continued burning releases carbon and destroys native habitat despite government restrictions.

nature-eco-701.title: Patch burning on Australian savannas
nature-eco-701.text: Lighting fires can cut emissions, if they are lit at the right time. Controlled burns on Australian savannas can produce a long-term cumulative reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. Burning early in the dry season makes a mosaic of burnt and unburnt land, and this patch burning reduces the area of stronger late dry-season fires. The West Arnhem Fire Management Agreement covers 28,000 square kilometers and partly offsets emissions from a liquefied natural gas plant in Darwin.

nature-eco-715.title: The criticism of FSC certification
nature-eco-715.text: FSC has been criticized since its founding, even by NGOs that once backed it. FERN (2011), Friends of the Earth UK (2008), ROBINWOOD (2009) and the Swedish Society for Nature Conservation (2011) withdrew their support. Critics argue that only large businesses can afford certification, producing a model of a few massive suppliers. FSC responded with a Small and Low Intensity Managed Forests standard. Resolute Forest Products, the largest manager of FSC-certified forests, was accused of logging on Barriere Lake Algonquin territory. FSC added a Quality Assurance Unit in 2013 and an online claims platform in 2014. It remains disputed whether FSC acts effectively on complaints and whether its model favors large firms.

nature-eco-714.title: Reading an FSC label: forest audit and chain of custody
nature-eco-714.text: FSC offers two kinds of certification, and only one lets a product carry its label. Forest management certification is voluntary: an accredited body inspects the forest at the owner's request, and holders pay an annual fee and must stay compliant. Chain of custody tracks certified material from forest to consumer, and only chain of custody holders may use FSC labels. The FSC Mix label, from 2004, lets manufacturers mix certified with uncertified material under controlled conditions. Unacceptable sources are excluded: illegal wood, wood harvested in violation of rights, and wood from HCV forests. FSC wood can earn up to 2 points in the LEED v4.1 credit Sourcing of Raw Materials.

nature-eco-716.title: Governing through the market instead of the state
nature-eco-716.text: No one can be fined or imprisoned for ignoring FSC. Non-state market driven governance is environmental governance outside state regulation that uses the market to drive sustainable management, and FSC is a leading example. The FSC network lacks the political authority of a state. Its power rests on buyers and sellers choosing to take part.

nature-eco-737.title: What shrinking oxygen does to fish and fisheries
nature-eco-737.text: When the ocean loses oxygen, fish lose room to live. Vertical expansion of tropical OMZs has reduced the oxygen-rich layer near the surface, so surface-dwelling fish could be affected periodically. Species with low tolerance of low oxygen are compressed into shallower water as the zones expand. Studies in the tropical Pacific and Atlantic found negative effects on fish populations and commercial fisheries, likely from habitat lost when the OMZ shoaled. This follows from {{ref:nature-eco-735}}, and the zones themselves are described in {{ref:nature-eco-736}}.

nature-eco-736.title: Oxygen minimum zones in the open ocean
nature-eco-736.text: Far below the surface, parts of the open ocean run short of oxygen naturally, because biological use outpaces supply. These are oxygen minimum zones, or OMZs. They typically lie at depths of about 200 to 1,000 meters, and their upper edge is a sharp oxygen gradient called the oxycline. Many persistent OMZs have thickened over five decades, as their upper limit became shallower and they expanded downward. Coastal and open-ocean oxygen-poor waters are highly interconnected, and both have grown in intensity, extent and duration.
